title: Moves Across Functions

writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
A parameter of type `String` takes ownership, while `&str` only borrows text. Read the signature before deciding whether the caller should keep using its value.

A function signature is an ownership map. `fn inspect(text: &str)` asks for temporary read access and lets the caller keep its `String`. `fn store(text: String)` takes ownership, so the caller cannot use that binding after the call unless the function returns it or the caller cloned it beforehand. A parameter like `i32` is passed by value too, but `i32` is `Copy`, which leaves the original usable. The syntax is the same; the type determines the effect.

Walk through the example: `name` owns its bytes, `&name` creates a borrowed view for `inspect`, and the borrow ends after its final use in the call. The last `println!` can therefore read `name`. Change `inspect` to accept `String` and pass `name` without `&`; the final print now triggers a move error. Returning a `String` is a legitimate design if the function transforms ownership, but a printing helper has no reason to consume its input.

When designing an API, use `&str` if any UTF-8 text view will do, `&String` only when the `String` container itself matters, and `String` when ownership or mutation independent of the caller is required. For mutable access without transfer, use `&mut String`. Try calling one borrowed helper with both a string literal and an owned string. The more flexible signature often makes the surrounding code simpler and avoids clones inserted only to satisfy an unnecessarily consuming function.
